To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the vast majority of 10 of 1o HLA‐A/B/C/DRB1/DQB1 matched unrelated donor‐recipient pairs have identical nucleotide sequences outside the ARD exonic regions; and (2) the few mismatches that occur are often silent and do not result in amino acid substitutions in the protein.
there was a very low frequency (0.39% overall) of HLA variation between donors and recipients outside of the ARDs.

there is limited HLA sequence variation between donor and recipients of hematopoietic cell transplantation outside the antigen recognition domain exonic sequences of HLA‐A and ‐B, ‐DQA1, ‐DQA2, ‐DQB2, ‐DRB, ‐DPA and ‐DPA2 genes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
HLA variation outside ARD exons in 10 of10 matched unrelated donor‐recipient pairs.
the frequency of variation in HLA alleles outside of the ARDs of matched unrelated donors and recipients and the effect on HSCT outcome.
the frequency and type of HLA variation outside of the ARDs in matched unrelated donor‐recipient pairs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is little variation in the HLA genes outside of the ARDs.
HLA mismatching outside the ARD is uncommon in 10 of10 matched donor‐recipient pairs and that the frequency of non‐ARD mismatching in the general donor population is unknown.
HLA variation between donor and recipients outside of the ARDs is rare and unlikely to impact outcomes of 10 of 1o matched HSCTs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is very limited variation in HLA alleles outside of the ARDs in unrelated donor HSCT pairs.
there is very little variation outside of the HLA antigen recognition region in the HLA‐A,B,C,DQA1,DQB1,DRB1 loci.
the HLA‐A and ‐B genes were the most variable, followed by ‐C and ‐DQB, with ‐DRB1 and ‐DQA1 being the least variable.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a very high degree of HLA allele matching between unrelated donor and recipient pairs for both the ARD and non‐ARD exonic regions.
the majority of HLA‐A/B/C/DRB1/DQB1 allele variation in HSCT donor‐recipient pairs occurs in the ARD exonic regions, which are the focus of current DNA typing methods.
the majority of the variation between donor and recipients is in the ARD exonic region, which has been the focus of DNA‐based HLA typing for HSCT.
